plan: Seven new SAT R&W items in the stricter design (measured WIC, nocebo inference with random assignment, bike-commuter counts versus shares, guild governance central idea, whom as an object, inverted had conditional, waggle-dance surprising result) plus S053-03 resubmitted as revision 2 (aphids instead of leaf-eating insects). Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: A bold report
passages.text: Though the committee's final report was ______ in tone, avoiding dramatic language and acknowledging the arguments on every side, its recommendations were bold: it called for closing two aging schools and building a new one.

passages.title: Warned about headaches
passages.text: In a study, volunteers were randomly assigned to take an inactive pill under one of two conditions. One group was told that the pill might cause headaches; the other group received the same pill without that warning. Volunteers who were warned reported headaches at about twice the rate of those who were not. These results suggest that ______

passages.title: Bike commuters
passages.text: In a city, 4 percent of the 200,000 workers commuted by bicycle in 2015. By 2023, the number of workers had grown to 300,000, and 6 percent of them commuted by bicycle. A transportation planner claims that the number of bicycle commuters more than doubled even though the share of workers who cycled rose by only half.

passages.title: Medieval guilds
passages.text: Historians once portrayed medieval craft guilds mainly as monopolies that protected their members by blocking new techniques. Recent studies of guild records paint a more mixed picture. Some guilds did suppress innovations that threatened their members, but others funded apprenticeships that spread skills and set quality standards that allowed distant buyers to trust unfamiliar goods. Whether a guild helped or hindered economic growth, these studies suggest, depended less on guilds as such than on how each one was governed.

passages.title: The new archivist
passages.text: The archivist ______ the library hired last spring has already digitized more than ten thousand letters from the town's founding families.

passages.title: Sensor drift
passages.text: Had the engineers ______ the sensor data more closely, they would have noticed the gradual drift in the readings weeks before the failure.

passages.title: The waggle dance
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Honeybees perform a "waggle dance" that tells nestmates the direction and distance of a food source.
- The dance was decoded in the mid-twentieth century by Karl von Frisch.
- Researchers later prevented some colonies from reading dance directions.
- In some seasons, those colonies gathered about as much food as colonies that could read the dances.
- In other seasons, colonies that could read the dances gathered noticeably more food.

passages.title: Red autumn leaves
passages.text:
Text 1
Why do some trees turn red in autumn rather than simply yellow? One botanist argues that the red pigments act as a sunscreen: as a leaf withdraws its nutrients before falling, the pigments shield it from sunlight damage, allowing the tree to recover more of those nutrients.

Text 2
Ecologists comparing tree species across regions found that trees with red autumn leaves are especially common where insects such as aphids, which lay their eggs on trees in autumn, are abundant. They propose that red coloring may advertise a tree's chemical defenses to these insects, discouraging them from laying eggs on it.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: avoiding dramatic language and acknowledging the arguments on every side
candidates.explanation: A report that avoids dramatic language and acknowledges all sides is calm and restrained, "measured" in tone, which contrasts with its bold recommendations.

A.rationale: "Exhaustive" describes thoroughness, but the text contrasts the report's calm tone with its bold content, not its completeness with anything.

B.rationale: Nothing concerns when the report appeared.

D.rationale: A report that acknowledges the arguments on every side is not partisan.

hints: What does "Though" contrast with the bold recommendations?
candidates.remember: Use the contrast signal and the description together.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: expectations alone can influence the symptoms that people report.
choices.B: the inactive pill contained an ingredient that tends to cause headaches.
choices.C: warnings about possible side effects should never be given to patients.
choices.D: the volunteers who were warned were more prone to headaches before the study.

candidates.evidence: the same pill without that warning
candidates.explanation: The pill and the assignment were the same for both groups; only the warning differed, so the expectation created by the warning is the likely cause of the extra reported headaches.

B.rationale: Both groups took the same inactive pill, so the pill cannot explain the difference.

C.rationale: The results describe an effect of warnings; they do not support a rule that warnings should never be given.

D.rationale: Random assignment makes a preexisting difference between the groups an unlikely explanation.

hints: What was different between the two groups?

strategy.explanation: Identify the single difference between the groups.

candidates.remember: When only one thing differs between randomly assigned groups, it is the likely cause.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the planner's claim?

choices.A: The share of workers who commuted by bicycle rose from 4 percent in 2015 to 6 percent in 2023.
choices.B: The city's workforce grew by 100,000 workers, from 200,000 in 2015 to 300,000 in 2023.
choices.C: By 2023, 18,000 of the city's 300,000 workers were commuting to their jobs by bicycle.
choices.D: Bicycle commuters rose from 8,000 to 18,000, while the share who cycled went from 4 to 6 percent.

candidates.evidence: the number of bicycle commuters more than doubled
candidates.explanation: 4 percent of 200,000 is 8,000 and 6 percent of 300,000 is 18,000, more than double, while the share rose from 4 to 6 percent, an increase of one-half. Only D gives both.

A.rationale: This supports the second half of the claim but gives no numbers of commuters.

B.rationale: Workforce growth alone does not show how many people cycled.

C.rationale: This gives the 2023 count but no 2015 count, so it cannot show the number more than doubled.

hints: What two facts does the claim combine?

strategy.explanation: Compute both counts, then compare with the shares.

candidates.remember: A count can change by a different factor than a percentage when the total changes.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Guilds mainly hindered growth by blocking new techniques, as historians have long held.
choices.B: Guilds' economic effects varied, depending largely on how each guild was governed.
choices.C: Guilds were chiefly responsible for spreading new skills across medieval Europe.
choices.D: Medieval buyers distrusted goods that were made outside their own towns.

candidates.evidence: depended less on guilds as such than on how each one was governed
candidates.explanation: The text replaces a uniform view of guilds with a mixed one and concludes that each guild's effect depended on its governance.

A.rationale: The text says recent studies complicate this older view.

C.rationale: The text says some guilds suppressed innovations, so this overstates their role.

D.rationale: This detail supports one point; it is not the text's main idea.

hints: What does the last sentence conclude?

strategy.explanation: Find the claim the examples support.

candidates.remember: Main ideas often appear as a conclusion after contrasting examples.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: Within the clause, "the library hired ___," the pronoun is the object of "hired," so the object form "whom" is correct.

B.rationale: "Who" is a subject form, but the archivist is the object of "hired" (the library hired whom).

C.rationale: "Whose" shows possession, but nothing here belongs to the archivist.

D.rationale: "Which" is not used to refer to a person in Standard English.

hints: Is the pronoun the subject or the object of "hired"?

strategy.explanation: Rearrange the clause: the library hired ___.

candidates.remember: Use "whom" for the object of a verb or preposition.
candidates.author_reason: withdrawn: who/whom is generally outside the Digital SAT conventions blueprint (solver note); not resubmitted

candidates.subskill: Verb form in an inverted conditional
candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: "Had the engineers examined" is an inverted form of "If the engineers had examined," which pairs with "would have noticed."

A.rationale: "Had" must be followed by a past participle; "examine" is the base form.

B.rationale: "Had have examined" is not a standard verb form.

D.rationale: "Examines" is a present-tense form and cannot follow "had."

candidates.remember: An inverted "Had" + subject + past participle means "If ... had."

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize a surprising finding about the usefulness of the waggle dance. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Karl von Frisch decoded the honeybee's waggle dance, which shows nestmates the direction and distance of food.
choices.B: Though the dance shows where food is, colonies unable to read it gathered about as much food in some seasons.
choices.C: In some seasons, colonies that could read the waggle dance gathered noticeably more food than others.
choices.D: Researchers prevented some honeybee colonies from reading the direction information in waggle dances.

candidates.evidence: those colonies gathered about as much food as colonies that could read the dances
candidates.explanation: The surprise is that a signal giving food locations sometimes made no difference to how much food colonies gathered. Only B pairs the dance's purpose with that result.

A.rationale: This describes the dance and its discoverer but not the surprising finding.

C.rationale: This is the expected result, not the surprising one.

D.rationale: This describes the method but not what the researchers found.

hints: What finding would be surprising, given what the dance does?

strategy.explanation: Look for a result that runs against expectation.

candidates.remember: To emphasize a surprise, pair the expectation with the result that defies it.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the ecologists in Text 2 most likely respond to the botanist's argument in Text 1?

choices.A: They would suggest that red coloring may serve a function other than the one Text 1 proposes.
choices.B: They would argue that red pigments provide no protection at all from sunlight damage.
choices.C: They would agree that red leaves protect against sunlight, which explains the regional pattern they found.
choices.D: They would argue that trees with yellow leaves are better at recovering nutrients in autumn.

candidates.evidence: They propose that red coloring may advertise a tree's chemical defenses
candidates.explanation: Text 2 offers a different explanation (signaling to insects) without disproving Text 1's; the ecologists would suggest red may serve another purpose.

B.rationale: The ecologists propose another function; they do not test or deny protection from sunlight.

C.rationale: Their explanation of the regional pattern involves insects, not sunlight.

D.rationale: Neither text compares nutrient recovery in yellow and red trees.

hints: Does Text 2 disprove Text 1 or offer an alternative?

strategy.explanation: Check whether Text 2 tests Text 1's claim.

candidates.remember: An alternative explanation is not the same as a refutation.

revision_history.reason: solver: the insect-signaling hypothesis concerns sap-feeding insects such as aphids, not leaf-eating insects; passage reworded, items unchanged
